To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the distribution of symbioses is controlled by climatic controls on the rate of decomposition and that the symbiotic nitrogen fixers are insensitive to the climatic controls on rate of decomposition.

the global distribution of tree symbiosis is driven by climate variables, and that ectomycorrizal trees dominate cold and dry climates, arbuscular-mycorrhizal (AM) trees dominate warm tropical climates, and symbiotic nitrogen-fixing trees dominate in dry and alkaline climates.

the global distribution of forest-tree symbiosis is primarily controlled by climate, and that ectomycorhizal symbiosis is most abundant in cold, seasonally dry climates, while arbuscular mycorrhzial symbiosis is most common in warm, seasonally wet climates, with symbiotic nitrogen fixation most common in dry, alkaline climates
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of symbiotic interactions in the distribution and abundance of plants, particularly trees.
the distribution of plant symbionts at a global scale.
the global distribution of tree symbiosises, and their climatic control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the symbiotic status and the symbiont identity of the dominant symbionts are determined primarily by climatic variables.
climate is the primary driver of the global distribution and abundance of symbiotic tree species, with the exception of symbiotic N fixers.

the global distribution of forest-tree symbiosis is controlled primarily by climatically controlled variation of decomposition rates, and that this variation in decomposition rate has a major impact on the global distribution of ectomycorrhiza.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distribution of symbioses is driven by climate variables and the distribution of ectomycorrhiza is driven by decomposition rate.

the global biogeographic patterns of symbioses between plants and fungi or bacteria are driven by climate, and that the global biotic gradient of symbiosis is controlled by climatic variation in the rate at which plant litter decomposes.
the distribution of major symbiotic associations is primarily controlled by climate variables, particularly the rate of decomposition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the symbiosis gradient is primarily controlled by climatic factors, and that symbioses are most likely to occur where climatic conditions are favourable to the symbionts.

climate variables are a primary driver of the global distribution and abundance of different symbiotic associations, and this distribution is largely driven by climatic controls on the rate of decomposition.
climate variables—in particular, climatically controlled variations in the rate of litter decomposition—are the primary driver of the global distribution and abundance of major tree symbioses.
